The three trait questions now open are deliberately separate and each can be answered alone: how large the vocabulary is, how many entries one person carries, and how often each entry appears. Answering any one of them is useful on its own.
A band is more useful than a number. A family that should appear in roughly a fifth of adults is actionable; 18.4 per cent is not, and would read as a measurement the game never made.

Clustering is worth a sentence if it applies. Some dispositions plausibly run in families or in a line of work, and the game already records both, so an answer that says where a trait concentrates can be used.
question: Across the few hundred people a player meets in one life, how common should each family of temperament traits be — which ones should turn up in most people, which in a handful, and which should be rare enough that meeting one is worth noticing?

title: How common each trait should be across a town
usableAnswer: A prevalence band per family in the catalogue's fourteen — roughly what share of adults should be marked with something from it — with the rare ones called out by name, and a line on whether any of them should cluster by circumstance rather than being spread evenly. The reasoning behind each band matters more than its exact figure, because the figure becomes a pack value a modder can change.
whyItMatters: Every generated person currently draws every trait from one seeded curve, so each pole is equally likely on everybody and the population is uniform by construction. A count alone does not fix that: if a person carries two traits drawn from a flat list, a town of three hundred still has no texture, because the same traits recur at the same rate everywhere. Prevalence is what makes a neighbourhood feel populated rather than sampled.
